crawler.headline: AI crawler docs consolidated, IP ranges published, and opt-out mechanisms expanded across major vendors.
crawler.body: Over the past year, AI crawler documentation has undergone a coordinated wave of consolidation and clarification. Major vendors—OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon, Google, and Common Crawl—have published or updated formal crawler-identification pages with explicit user-agent strings, IP-range JSON endpoints, and semantically distinct opt-out mechanisms (robots.txt directives, meta tags, and page-level headers). The most significant operational shift is the emergence of machine-readable IP allowlists (`googlebot.json` renamed to `common-crawlers.json`, new CCBot CIDR blocks, Anthropic's first-ever published ranges), enabling webmasters to implement IP-based verification at scale. Simultaneously, site-level opt-out granularity has expanded: Amazon's `noarchive` meta tag, Google-Extended's distinction, and OpenAI's new `OAI-AdsBot` disclosure all signal a move toward per-crawler control rather than blanket allow/block decisions. Infrastructure tooling—Cloudflare's AI Crawl Control, pay-per-crawl, and canonical-redirect features—has matured in parallel, giving publishers and operators new levers for monetization and content-steering. The adoption of emerging standards like `llms.txt` by major vendors (Perplexity) suggests convergence on machine-readable index structures. Collectively, these changes reduce ambiguity around crawler identity and intent, though they demand active upkeep from operators managing IP allowlists and bot-detection rules.

ecosystem.headline: AI agent traffic surges, pushing bot detection and publisher scraping protections to the center of platform infrastructure.
ecosystem.body: The last 30 days revealed two colliding forces reshaping the content ecosystem. On the regulation side, the EU moved toward simplified AI rules while banning certain harmful applications, and publishers (via the News Media Alliance) escalated legal action against unauthorized scraping—filing an amicus brief supporting Amazon's case against Perplexity and demanding Common Crawl establish stronger protections. Simultaneously, the infrastructure layer shifted dramatically as DataDome reported a 50x surge in model context protocol (MCP) traffic following Anthropic's connector expansion, signaling that agentic AI access to web content is now mainstream. In response, DataDome rolled out a suite of new controls—Priority Protect, Agent Trust governance, intent-based policies, and vendor evaluation frameworks—positioning bot and agent triage as essential infrastructure. The ecosystem is essentially bifurcating: regulators are tightening rules around harmful uses, publishers are fighting unauthorized data extraction through legal channels, and middleware vendors are racing to build the detection and governance layer that makes agent-at-scale feasible.

agent.headline: Codex agents move from sandbox to production with security frameworks in place.
agent.body: The past month shows AI agent infrastructure moving from experimental to production-ready. OpenAI released a Windows sandbox environment for Codex agents, then quickly followed with a formal security and compliance framework—signaling confidence in the stack's maturity. Real-world validation arrived with Sea Limited's deployment across engineering teams, demonstrating that code-generation agents can operate at scale within enterprise workflows. In parallel, the ecosystem is broadening: Parloa voice agents became integrated into OpenAI's platform, suggesting bot-identity standards are beginning to encompass modalities beyond text. The sequence reflects a maturing narrative: infrastructure → guardrails → adoption.
